source: original; stimulus paraphrased from the Rosenberg espionage case, 1950-1953

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Rosenberg espionage case, 1950-1953. Paraphrased, not quoted, because the source is after 1929.
stimulus.text: In 1950, Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were arrested and charged with passing secrets about the atomic bomb to the Soviet Union. Both were members of the Communist Party, and both insisted they were innocent. They were convicted of espionage and sentenced to death. Despite pleas for clemency from around the world, they were executed in the electric chair in 1953.

stem: The executions were controversial in part because

options.text: Ethel was less implicated than Julius but got the same sentence.
Both Rosenbergs confessed to espionage before they died.
options.misconception: Both Rosenbergs insisted they were innocent to the end. A confession would have ended the controversy, not fed it.

options.text: The Supreme Court overturned the guilty verdicts before the executions took place.
options.misconception: The Supreme Court did not overturn the verdicts. The executions went ahead in 1953 despite pleas for clemency.

options.text: The Rosenbergs were never brought to trial at all.
options.misconception: The Rosenbergs were tried, convicted, and sentenced. The controversy was about the trial and the sentence, not about the absence of a trial.

rationales.A: Background from the books: Julius was more deeply implicated than his wife, yet both were convicted and sentenced to death. The equal punishment for unequal roles troubled many observers.
rationales.B: Both Rosenbergs insisted they were innocent to the end. A confession would have ended the controversy, not fed it.
rationales.C: The Supreme Court did not overturn the verdicts. The executions went ahead in 1953 despite pleas for clemency.
rationales.D: The Rosenbergs were tried, convicted, and sentenced. The controversy was about the trial and the sentence, not about the absence of a trial.
rationales.general:
1. Background from the books: Two defendants stood trial together for the same crime, but their roles in the spy ring were not equal.
2. Background from the books: Julius was more deeply implicated in the espionage than his wife.
3. Background from the books: Yet both received the same sentence, death, and the equal punishment for unequal roles troubled many observers.
Remember: When punishment ignores differences in guilt, the sentence itself becomes the argument.
